newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM defies pressure in racism row.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM defies pressure in racism row.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard strongly attacked racism on Tuesday, but defied pressure to reject anti-Aboriginal and anti-Asian remarks by a rebel politician that have struck a chord with voters.
"I will always denounce racial intolerance," the leader of the ruling Liberal-National coalition told parliament during a question time offensive by the Labor opposition.
"The Liberal and National parties will yield to nobody, no political force in this country, in our commitment for racial equality and racial tolerance."

Labor and industry and community leaders have urged Howard to publicly repudiate anti-Aboriginal and anti-Asian comments by independent politician Pauline Hanson, who was dumped from the Liberal Party this year after a string of controversial remarks.

Lower house member Hanson, a fish-and-chip shop owner from socially and politically conservative Queensland state, said in her maiden parliamentary speech a month ago that Asian immigrants were "swamping" Australia.
She also said Asian countries posed a military threat and has made a series of anti-Aboriginal comments. Howard, while rejecting racism itself, refused in parliament to repudiate Hanson's comments.

Opposition Labor leader Kim Beazley warned that her remarks would hurt many Australians and damage the country's standing with important Asian trading partners. But an opinion poll in Tuesday's Sydney Morning Herald newspaper showed 48 percent of Australians backed Hanson's comments, compared with 38 percent who opposed her stand.

Other polls have also showed that many Australians believe the country is accepting too many migrants from Asia, and anti-immigration candidates such as Hanson have been winning increasing electoral support.
Asians make up about 25 percent of the 100,000 migrants who arrive each year.

Australia's first Chinese member of parliament, Helen Sham-Ho of the New South Wales state Liberal opposition, warned that Howard's failure to repudiate Hanson could fuel suspicions that he was afraid of upsetting people who held similar views.
Asked in a radio interview last week if he believed any of Hanson's comments, Howard said: "I thought some of the things she said were an accurate reflection of what people feel."

Australia's main tourist industry group, the Tourism Task Force, said at the weekend it had written to Howard urging him to speak out against Hanson to protect Australia's image abroad, especially in key Asian markets.
"For the sake of economic reality and cultural responsibility, as prime minister you must publicly condemn the comments of Ms Hanson," Task Force head Chris Brown wrote.
"While we appreciate your stance that Ms Hanson should not dictate your agenda, we cannot allow the rest of the world to think of us as 'white trash' or a nation of 'rednecks'."
Howard told parliament there should be more public debate about Australia's immigration policies.
"People are entitled to attack the present immigration level without being branded bigots or racists," he said.

"(But) no matter what arguments there may be about immigration policy in this country, once a person has come to this country, that person is entitled to the respect that is due every other Australian, irrespective of that person's background."
